To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) vanA-containing enteroccocci of animal origin are genetically related to human isolates, (ii) the vanA gene cluster is present in two distinct forms (Tn1546 and Tn1549), and (iii) Tn1546 is the dominant form in enterococci from humans, animals and food.

1) the Tn1546 structure is highly variable and the genetic diversity is greater than previously reported; 2) vanA-containing enteroccoci from humans and animals have a different genetic background than those isolated from food; 3) the vanA-containing entercocci isolated from humans and animals belong to a different clonal complex than those isolated from animals.

(i) Tn1546 is a complex transposon, containing a large insertion sequence (IS) element, and (ii) vanA-containing enteroccoci of animal, human, and food origin belong to a small number of sequence types.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of new methods for the detection and identification of enterococcal strains, the development of new typing methods for enterococci and the investigation of enterococci from food and clinical sources for the presence of antibiotic resistance genes and virulence factors.
the molecular epidemiology of enterococci and the genetic basis of antibiotic resistance in these organisms.
the development and application of new methods and tools for the detection of antibiotic resistance in bacteria and the characterization of antibiotic resistant bacteria in the environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
vancomycin resistance is not a significant issue in the treatment of enterococcal infections in humans.

the vanA gene cassette and its surrounding Tn1546 transposon is the most important genetic element responsible for vancomycin resistance in Enterococci, and the most important genetic determinant of vancomycin resistance of Enterococci in clinical settings.
the presence of vanA gene is the main cause of the resistance in Enterococcus spp., and that the presence of Tn1546 is a good indicator of the presence of the gene.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed an efficient and reliable PCR assay for detection and differentiation of the vanA gene in enterococci and have determined the genetic structure of vanA-containing Enterococcus faecium and E faecalis.
we are trying to understand the evolution of antibiotic resistance and the spread of resistance genes in bacteria, and how this impacts on public health.
we were able to identify a number of vanA-containing E. faecium and E. faecalis isolates from animal, human and foods.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have shown that the presence of a vanA-containing Tn1546 in a clinical Enterococcus faecalis strain is not a sufficient condition for the development of a vancomycin-resistant phenotype.
we need to be careful when interpreting data from the gut microbiome and to consider the possibility that our results could be confounded by the presence of antibiotic residues.
the vanA gene cluster is highly variable in structure.
